title: The lab, the store and the engine refuse what the security audit found they accepted
description: Closes every finding of the 2026-09-11 security audit of the lab, the board store and the engine (OWASP Top 10 and OWASP CI/CD Top 10 as the checklist). Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-11-security-hardening-design.md`, plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-11-security-hardening.md`. ## What was wrong - **F1 (Medium, A01, CWE-22/352):** `POST /api/boards` passed a string `seed` into the board id, and `join()` resolved its `..`, so a request could write `.json`, `.board.json` and `.svg` files outside the store. The server did not check `Origin`, so a page on another localhost port could send that request (CSRF). - **F2 (Medium, A03, CWE-79):** the Library tab put `meta.source`, `meta.id` and error messages into `innerHTML`. Combined with F1, this was a stored XSS in the lab origin. - **Lower:** no Host check (DNS rebinding); the whole of `packages/cli/` was served; no security headers; an unbounded body and view, metrics and command fields; unscoped Deno permissions; CI actions pinned by mutable tags; `toSvg` spread one array per highlighted piece into a single call; `voidFrac` ≥ 1 looped forever; no credential ignores ahead of the Firebase slice. ## What changed - **Engine:** - a new envelope rule, `wholeNumbers`: width, height and seed must be whole numbers, and the CLI and the lab refuse `--seed=1.5` with exit code 2 and a translated reason; - the Carver refuses a `voidFrac` outside `[0, 1)`; - `toSvg` highlights any number of pieces without spreading them into one call. - **Lab server:** - **What a POST may store:** params are rebuilt from the `PARAM_SPEC` knobs and validated; view, metrics, command and source are checked by type and bound; SVG uploads are refused; the body is capped at 16 MiB. - **Who may send requests:** loopback hosts only; writes from another origin are refused; a POST must carry `Content-Type: application/json`. - **What is served:** only `lab.html`, `dist/` and `boards/`, with a CSP on the page, a sandbox CSP on stored files, and `nosniff`, `no-referrer`, `CORP` and `DENY` framing on every response. - **Store:** `saveBoard` refuses an id that is not `seed-<8 hex>`. - **Lab page:** every value from the store, a board file or an error goes through `escapeHtml` before it joins markup. - **Permissions:** - the lab server gets the network on 127.0.0.1, read of its directory and the store, write of the store, and one environment variable; - carve, compile and the docs image script read their four environment variables by name. - **CI and repository:** actions are pinned by commit SHA, with Dependabot watching them; `.env*` and service-account files are ignored; both READMEs say which hooks the repository runs in Claude Code. ## Behaviour changes to know about - A board saved before this branch whose stored params fall outside today's envelope, or lack a knob, is refused when you save a new view of it from the Library. The page shows only "not saved". New boards are unaffected. - The lab server no longer serves source files next to the page (for example `/carve.ts`). It also no longer accepts an SVG in a POST: the lab never sent one, and the CLI still saves previews directly. - No generated board changes: `fingerprints.json`, `svg-golden.json` and the Node smoke test are untouched and green. ## Found on the way, left for a separate change The review of this branch turned up an engine bug outside its scope: with `voidFrac > 0` the Carver's `remaining` stops matching the free-cell count (43 of 120 runs drift at `voidFrac` 0.1, one run ended at `remaining = -1`), because the void target is subtracted even when fewer voids were placed. Nothing here reaches it: `voidFrac` is not a `PARAM_SPEC` knob, the lab never sets it, and the server forces it back to its default. ## Verification - `deno task verify` and `pnpm nx run-many -t verify` are green. - A live check in Chrome ran the lab with `lab.sh`'s scoped flags. Generating, auto-saving, opening a board in the Library, recolouring, deleting, exporting SVG and switching language all worked, with no CSP violations in the console. I then planted `` as a stored `source`: it showed as plain text and nothing ran.

title: SVG off the main thread: the lab exports in a worker, --dry-run draws none
description:
Two follow-ups from the review of #40.

## `--dry-run` draws no SVG

The dry run rendered a full SVG only to report its size (`svgBytes`). Boards are stored as board files now, and the JSON line already carries the board file's size in `boardBytes`, so the render and the field are gone. `carve.test.ts` asserts the line has no `svgBytes`; `HISTORY.md` and the `carve.ts` comment say so.

## The lab's SVG export runs in a worker

"Download SVG" used to call `toSvg` on the page's thread (tens of megabytes of text on the largest boards). It now starts a one-shot instance of `lab-worker.js`, sends it the board file and the view (`WorkerIn` `{ type: 'svg', board, options }`), and gets the text back (`WorkerOut` `{ type: 'svg', svg }`). It is not the generation worker: `run()` terminates that one on every new run, and its queue would hold the export back until the run ends. The button is disabled while the export is drawn.

Found while testing: exporting during a run named the file after the run in progress (`runParams` moves on at run start) while the content was the board on screen. The name now comes from `labParams`, set when a board arrives.

## Measured

Chrome, 400×400, lab on this branch: 3.77 MB SVG, 102 ms click to download, no long tasks on the main thread (largest gap between 16 ms ticks: 17 ms). Export during a running generation downloads the previous board under its own seed.

## Checks

- `deno task verify`: 185 passed
- `pnpm nx run-many -t verify`: green

title: The CLI writes a board file by default, and the board element and the lab draw from it
description:
## Why

A board existed only as the output of `generate(params)`. The store kept an SVG picture plus a recipe, so drawing or playing a board meant running the generator first. That takes about 10 s in Node and about 27 s in a Chrome worker for Insane. To pregenerate boards and keep them in Cloud Storage, with metadata in Firestore, a board has to become a file. Firebase itself is out of scope here.

Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-11-board-data-model-design.md` · Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-11-board-data-model.md`

## What changes

- **Engine**
  - `BoardData { W, H, owner, pieces }` is what every reader needs, and `Board extends BoardData`. `fingerprint`, `toSvg`, `analyse`, `render`, `voidStrips` and the game take `BoardData`.
  - New runtime-neutral `board-file.ts` with `encodeBoard` and `decodeBoard`. A file is a readable JSON header (`format`, `v`, `W`, `H`, counts, `fingerprint`) around a base64 body: varint piece headers, 2-bit steps, void deltas.
  - `decodeBoard` refuses any file that is not a board this engine can read and says why. That covers malformed base64, a truncated or overlong body, a piece leaving the board, overlapping pieces, a piece on a void, a repeated id or an out-of-range id, header counts that disagree with the body, and a fingerprint mismatch.
- **CLI** (`carve.ts`, `store.ts`, `command.ts`)
  - The default output is `<id>.board.json` + `<id>.json`. `--svg` adds the preview and `--svg=path` also writes a copy.
  - New `--advanced --board` mode. `buildCommand` writes `--board`; old `--advanced --svg` commands keep working.
  - New batch mode, `--count=N [--max-seeds=M]`: N closed boards on consecutive seeds. Seeds that do not close are skipped and not stored, and the run gives up after `2·N` seeds by default.
  - `BoardMeta` gains `fingerprint`, `boardBytes` and `svg`, and drops `svgBytes`.
- **Lab**
  - Both tabs draw through `<arrowz-board>`, imported from `../board-element/src/mod.ts`.
  - The worker only generates and posts the board file. The page decodes it, draws it, builds the longest-pieces table, and makes the SVG only on "Download SVG".
  - The library opens board files and saves a new view without regenerating.
  - The lab's own zoom and fit controls are gone; the element pans and zooms.
  - The server's `POST /api/boards` takes a board file, validates it by decoding, and stores it canonically.
- **Board element**: takes `BoardData`. The demo worker posts a board file instead of copying seven fields around `DataCloneError`.
- **Docs**: README EN and PL (the board file is the default, the picture sits behind `--svg`, batch mode) and CLAUDE.md.

## Measured (Apple M1, Insane 1000×1000, seed 7, 85 809 pieces)

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Board file | 884 750 B (the SVG is 21.7 MB) |
| `decodeBoard` | 111 ms median in Deno 2.9; 81 ms on Chrome 152's main thread |
| Board arrival in the lab | one ~740 ms main-thread task, 548 ms of it the element's first draw (tessellation 414 ms, upload 114 ms). That draw is the next bottleneck; it was not added here |

## Heads-up

- `deno task check`, `deno task bundle`, `deno task verify` and `lab.sh` now need `corepack enable pnpm && pnpm install` once. The lab bundles the element, which resolves Lit from `packages/board-element/node_modules`. `lab.sh` checks for it and prints the hint.
- Boards stored before this change have only an SVG, so they drop out of the lab's list. Each one can be reproduced from its command.
- #39 retypes the same GL files (`gl-layer.ts`, `tesselate.ts`, `gl-passes.ts`), which this PR moves from `Board` to `BoardData`. Whichever lands second gets a small type-import conflict.

## Verification

- `deno task verify`: 185 tests pass.
- `pnpm nx run-many -t verify`: all 3 projects pass, including the engine's Node smoke test (which now round-trips every golden board through the file) and the board element's Vitest suite in Chromium.
- The golden fingerprints and SVG hashes are unchanged.
- Lab checked in Chrome through DevTools with synthetic input. Panning, wheel zoom and the fit button still need a pass with a real mouse.

title: One instanced disc draws every tail cap and round join
description:
Pass 3 of the three agreed after #34: every arrow's tail cap and every rounded corner on `<arrowz-board>` is now one primitive — a disc `(cx, cy, r)` drawn as an instance of a shared unit quad, its edge computed in the fragment shader — instead of triangle fans (48 vertices a tail, 21 a corner).

Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-11-disc-primitive-design.md` (§10 has the measurements). Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-11-disc-primitive.md`.

## Why one primitive

The export draws corners with `stroke-linejoin="round"`, which by the SVG definition is a full disc of radius half the stroke on the vertex, and tails with `<circle>`. So a corner and a tail are the same thing, and the three quarters of a corner disc the old quarter fan left out lie under the two segments anyway.

## What changed

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `tesselate.ts` | A second stream beside the unchanged triangles: `Scene.discs` (3 floats a disc) in the same four blocks; `PieceRanges.corners/tail`; `tesselatePiece` returns `{ vertices, discs }`; `rideDiscBound`; `Scene.cornerRadius`. The fans (`TAIL_SEGMENTS`, `JOIN_SEGMENTS`, `writeDisc`, `writeJoin`) are deleted. Each polyline is merged once per piece. |
| `gl-shaders.ts` | `DISC_VERT` / `DISC_FRAG` (highp): quad widened by half a device pixel, analytic one-pixel edge, sub-pixel discs faded by their size, `r <= 0` collapses to no fragment. |
| `gl-resources.ts` | Disc program, disc buffer, unit-quad buffer, lazy disc colour and rider disc buffers; `writeRange` collapses discs too. |
| `gl-passes.ts` | Each block's discs drawn right after its triangles, via `drawArraysInstanced` with the attribute pointer moved to the block's first disc (WebGL2 has no `baseInstance`); attribute state left as found. Corner blocks under half a device pixel of radius are skipped on the CPU. Riders draw their discs inside the same scissor. |
| `rides.ts` | `Rider` carries its discs; both bounds checked. |

`--sharp`, the engine, the CLI and the public API of `GlLayer` and `<arrowz-board>` are unchanged.

## Measured (Insane 1000×1000, seed 7; real Chrome headless on an M1 with its GPU, dpr 2; GPU timer query, median of 15, runs alternated)

| | `main` | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Static data, monochrome | 102.9 MB | **27.9 MB** |
| Extra with colours on | 51.5 MB | **13.2 MB** |
| `setBoard` | 424-627 ms | **135-222 ms** |
| GPU a frame, fitted zoom | 8.3-9.9 ms | **5.7-5.9 ms** |
| GPU a frame, fitted, coloured | 9.7-11.7 ms | **6.8-6.9 ms** |
| GPU a frame, `MAX_CELL_PX` | 6.6-8.4 ms | 6.4-7.3 ms |

The first cut was 2.4 ms slower than `main` at the fitted zoom. Two measured changes fixed that: the quad margin went from a whole pixel to half (the edge's ramp only reaches that far), and corner discs under half a pixel are skipped (below that, three quarters lie under the segments and the rest is at most a quarter of a pixel).

Screenshots against `main`: no difference the eye finds at `MAX_CELL_PX` or 8 px a cell; the fitted zoom matches in tone. Translucent (`rgba`) ink was already wrong on `main` (every overlap composites twice) and is wrong differently here; ruled not a supported look (spec §9).

## New tests

- True-circle pixel probes zoomed far past `MAX_CELL_PX` (a tail and a corner, static and riding): ink where a fan's facet left paper. Written before the fans were deleted, so they are what makes the deletion safe.
- A ridden-out piece leaves no disc behind; a restored context draws discs again; the diagnostic hue and highlight reach discs.
- A frame leaves no instanced divisor on any attribute location and the main program current, checked red by removing the divisor reset.
- Sub-pixel corner blocks are skipped and tails are not, per block (a highlighted piece crosses the threshold at its own zoom).

## Verification

- `pnpm nx run-many -t verify`: green (board-element node 153, chromium 114 + 4 skipped).
- `deno task verify`: green (165).

title: Split gl-layer.ts by responsibility
description:
Pass 2 of the three agreed after #34: a pure refactor of `packages/board-element/src/gl-layer.ts` (1 047 lines) into modules by responsibility, so that pass 3 (one round primitive in the fragment shader for the tail cap and the corners) lands in the shader and pass modules and leaves the context's life alone.

Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-11-split-gl-layer-design.md`. Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-11-split-gl-layer.md`.

## Modules

| File | Holds | Lines |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gl-layer.ts` | the facade: context taken, lost, handed back and given up; board and view state; the order of a frame | 513 |
| `gl-shaders.ts` | the GLSL sources and `link` | 85 |
| `gl-color.ts` | `Rgba`, `rgbaOf`, `hueRgba` | 48 |
| `rides.ts` | `Rides`, the ride clock, behind an eight-call `RideHost` | 240 |
| `gl-resources.ts` | `GlResources`: every GL object and every write into one, listed once instead of three times | 146 |
| `gl-passes.ts` | the frame's passes as free functions | 197 |
| `tesselate.ts` | gains `voidQuads` | |

## What does not change

- `GlLayer`'s public surface: no member is added, removed or re-typed.
- `arrowz-board.ts` is untouched, and so is every existing test. The only diff to `*.test.ts` is three new `voidQuads` cases.
- A frame makes the same GL calls in the same order. The one exception: the dot pass sets its three view uniforms through the shared `setView`, which produces the same values.

## The one deliberate difference (spec §3.2)

`GlResources.create` returns the whole set of programs and buffers, or throws before anything is assigned. Before, a throw from `link` part way through `acquire` left a partial set. The shaders are constants, so this path can only be reached by a driver that rejects them.

## New test

`rides.browser.test.ts` pins spec §4.1: cancelling a ride never asks for a frame. Before this branch no test guarded that rule, and adding `schedule()` to `cancelRunning` turned nothing red. The split made the test cheap to write, because `Rides` takes a stub host. It was checked by adding the forbidden `schedule()` and watching it go red.

## Verification

- `pnpm nx run-many -t verify`: green. board-element: 17 files, 252 passed, 4 skipped (was 247). Engine: 165 passed.
- `ARROWZ_MEASURE=1` perf, headless, before and after:

  | Measure | Before | After |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Insane build | 506 ms | 482 ms |
  | Insane build, grid off | 483 ms | 494 ms |
  | Insane build, grid on | 423 ms | 442 ms |
  | Coloured ride | 585 ms | 586 ms |

  Pans and zooms stay at vsync (16.7 ms), so the headless run cannot show a change there. All differences are within run-to-run spread.
- Still to do before merge: a manual pass over the demo with a real mouse (spec §7).

title: nx.json ends with a newline, so deno task verify reaches its tests again
description:
One byte: a trailing newline at the end of `nx.json`.

## Why

Nx wrote the analytics opt-out into `nx.json` in `905000c` and left the file
without a final newline. The root `deno task verify` is
`check && lint && fmt && test`, and `deno fmt --check` covers the whole
workspace, so it failed on `nx.json` and the chain stopped before `test`.
Since then `deno task verify` has not run the engine and CLI tests at all;
a real test failure would have been hidden behind a formatting error.

`pnpm nx run-many -t verify` did not notice, because each project's `fmt`
target checks only its own files.

## Gates

- `deno task verify` exits 0 and reaches its tests: 165 passed, 0 failed.
- `pnpm nx run-many -t verify`: 3 projects, 16 tasks, all green; the run
  leaves `nx.json` untouched.

## If it comes back

Should Nx rewrite the file without the newline again, the lasting fix is to
exclude `nx.json` from `deno fmt` in the root `deno.json` rather than to
keep adding the byte back.

title: A plain drag pans, and the board survives what the demo sweep threw at it
description:
Stacked on #34 (itself on #33): the WebGL layer and the corner chrome are not on
`main` yet, so this branches off `feat/rounded-arrows` and should merge there
first.

Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-11-board-hardening-design.md`
Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-11-board-hardening.md`

## Why

A sweep of the demo, driven live in Chrome, turned up seven failures. Every one
was reproduced on the page before it was designed against:

1. Sixteen `document.createElement('arrowz-board')` calls, never connected,
   evicted a visible board's WebGL context, and the board stayed blank for good.
2. After a drag whose `pointerup` never arrived, plain hover kept panning.
3. With the board focused, ⌘/Ctrl + `-`, `+`, `0` stopped zooming the page.
4. `pad="abc"`, `view.stroke: NaN` and a `point-radius` of 5 drew a blank, a
   broken or a flooded board, and `viewport-change` handed the host `NaN`.
5. The host's height depended on its history (a 20×3000 host left it
   228 750 px tall), because the canvas lent it an intrinsic size.
6. One touch that never ended turned every later tap into a pinch.
7. The demo opened on an empty board.

## What changes

**A plain drag pans, and a ⌘/Ctrl click plays** (mouse and pen). A plain click
does nothing, so a hand that twitches while panning never costs a life. A
playable board shows a ☝ switch in the corner that restores the old rule. The
choice belongs to the player: it is kept in `localStorage['arrowz-board.gestures']`
and readable as `gestureMode`, and there is no attribute. A board that only pans
has no switch and always pans with a plain drag. Touch is unchanged. On macOS a
Ctrl click is a secondary click, so where it plays the context menu stays shut.

**A move that reports the button up is the release.** A mouse or pen move with
no button held ends the press the way `pointerup` would. That fixes the sticky
pan, and it also keeps clicks alive when the browser reports the button up in a
move before the `pointerup`. Chrome under automation does exactly that: the first
version of this rule (reset on such a move) lost every ⌘-click in the live demo.
A lost pointer capture, or the window losing focus mid-press, cancels the
gesture. A primary touch drops any stale touch.

**The context is taken on connect, and asked back.** `GlLayer` no longer takes a
context in its constructor, so elements that are created and never connected
cost nothing. If the browser takes a connected board's context, the board asks
for it back as soon as an `IntersectionObserver` sees it on screen. More than
about sixteen boards on screen at once will take each other's contexts in turn;
that is the browser's ceiling.

**Nonsense draws the default.** A pure `sanitize.ts` corrects what reaches the
layer and the viewport:

- a value that is not a finite number becomes its default;
- `stroke` is kept within (0, 1];
- head sizes and `pad` are never negative;
- `top` is a whole count;
- `point-radius` is kept within [0, 0.5];
- a colour the browser cannot parse becomes its field's default.

Properties and attributes keep what the host set. `pad` and `point-radius` use
Lit's `useDefault`, because the reflect scheduled by the constructor's default
otherwise overwrote `pad="abc"` with `"NaN"`. `zoomBy` ignores a factor that is
not a finite positive number.

**Keys with ⌘, Ctrl or Alt belong to the browser**, and no key is taken while
there is nothing to zoom.

**The canvas is out of the layout.** The host has no size of its own, like a
`<div>`. The demo gives it a definite height and generates a board on load.

## Breaking for consumers

- The default mouse and pen rule changed (plain click no longer plays).
- `BoardLabels` lost `panHintMac` and `panHintOther`, in favour of `dragHint`,
  `dragPlayHintMac`/`dragPlayHintOther`, `clickHintMac`/`clickHintOther` and
  `gesturesMac`/`gesturesOther`.
- A host that relied on an unsized `<arrowz-board>` taking the canvas's
  height now gets a 0 px tall host.
- A fresh element no longer carries `pad="4"` as an attribute.

No consumer of `@arrowz/board-element` exists in the repository outside its
demo.

## Measured

Insane 1000×1000, seed 7 (85 809 pieces), foreground Chrome, the demo's
Measure button:

| | pan mean / worst | zoom mean / worst |
| --- | --- | --- |
| this branch | 33.3 / 34.0 ms | 33.3 / 34.3 ms |

This is the same as before the branch (the WebGL spec records about 34 ms).
The main-thread cost of rebuilds on Insane (220–500 ms per view change,
369 ms `restart()`, 724 ms `loadState()`) is out of scope and gets its own
design.

## Verification

- [x] `pnpm nx run-many -t verify`: 3 projects, 16 tasks, green. board-element:
  247 passed, 4 skipped (perf, measure-only).
- [x] `packages/engine`: check, lint and 165 tests green, `fingerprints.test.ts`
  included; the engine is not touched.
- [x] Demo, driven by hand in Chrome:
  - a plain drag pans, and a plain click plays nothing;
  - ⌘-click plays exactly once;
  - ☝ switches to click mode, a plain click plays, and the choice survives a reload;
  - 20 orphan elements leave the board drawn;
  - `pad="abc"` keeps the board.
- [x] **macOS Ctrl-click** plays without a context menu: checked by hand in
  the demo (automation cannot send a native secondary click).
- [ ] Not from this branch: `deno task verify` in `packages/engine` fails on
  the formatting of the root `nx.json` (missing trailing newline), which is on
  `main` since 905000c.

title: Rounded arrows, a literal head height, and a harmless slip of the finger
description:
Stacked on #33: the WebGL layer is not on `main` yet, so this branches off
`feat/webgl-board-layer` and should merge there first.

Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-10-rounded-arrows-design.md`
Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-10-rounded-arrows.md`

## What changes

**A piece can turn through a rounded corner.** A new `rounded` view field,
defaulting to true — which is what `toSvg` has always drawn, so the export is
unchanged and the WebGL board catches up to it. False gives mitred corners and
a square tail cap of the same reach, so a piece occupies the same length either
way. The head stays a sharp polygon in both modes: `rounded` means exactly what
`stroke-linejoin` plus the tail cap mean in SVG, which is what lets the export
honour it without inventing geometry.

**The rounding is free, and it was measured before it was chosen.** A quarter
fan of seven facets at each real corner, paid for by collapsing collinear runs
first. On Insane 1000x1000 seed 7 (85 809 pieces), GPU time per frame with
`EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2` around every `drawArrays`, three samples:

| shape | vertices/frame | GPU ms/frame | mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| before this branch | 10.38 M | 17.61 / 16.97 / 16.79 | **17.12** |
| fan, no merge | 15.35 M | 18.50 / 18.40 / 17.67 | 18.19 |
| **fan + merge (shipped)** | 12.04 M | 17.17 / 17.57 / 16.65 | **17.13** |

Noise band about +/-0.9 ms. Two thirds of a polyline's interior points are not
corners at all — `pieceShape` pushes every cell centre in, so a piece running
straight through six cells carried five 180-degree joins costing two triangles
each and changing nothing.

**The arrowhead height is a number, not a mode.** `headHeight: 0` no longer
means "work it out from the stroke"; it is literal, and the default is one cell
in both the CLI's `View` and the element's `BoardView`. `headWidth` keeps its
automatic mode at 0. `--headheight=0` now draws a head of no height, on purpose:
silently reinterpreting a number the user typed is worse than drawing what they
asked for. Boards saved before this change carry `headHeight: 0` and are read as
unset, the way `store.ts` already handles knobs that did not exist yet.

**One set of ranges.** The demo offered `stroke` 0.05 to 1.5 and both head knobs
0 to 3; the lab had capped `stroke` at 0.9 since it was written. Both now offer
`stroke` 0.2 to 0.9, `headWidth` 0 to 0.9, `headHeight` 0.1 to 1, step 0.05.

**A slipped finger costs nothing.** A double click used to reset the view and
click the arrow underneath; a double tap used to reset the view. A second press
at the same place inside the double window now yields no intent at all, on mouse,
pen and touch. The first press still plays its piece — suppressing that too would
mean holding every press for 300 ms. `fit()` keeps the corner button and the `0`
key.

**`--sharp`,** in both CLI dialects and in the lab, with the label translated.

**The README images can be made again.** Deleting the automatic height changed
every committed image, and nothing recorded the commands that made them. This
adds `docs/images/manifest.json`, a recorder, and `deno task docs`. 30 of 34
images regenerated; re-running the recorder on a clean tree returns them byte
for byte, SVG and PNG.

## What is deliberately not done

- `rule-free`, `rule-blocked` and `rule-shape` are hand-made composites with a
  drawn grid `toSvg` never emits, and `scale-1000-detail` is a hand-cut window
  whose crop origin is unrecoverable. All four are recorded in the manifest's
  `handMade` list with reasons and printed on every run. Their arrowheads still
  follow the deleted rule and read slightly shorter than everything else.
- Splitting `gl-layer.ts`, and moving the round primitive into the fragment
  shader, are the next two passes. The prize there is the tail disc, not the
  corners: 48 vertices a piece, 4.12 M of this branch's 12.04 M.

## Gates

`pnpm nx run-many -t verify` — 16 of 16 tasks green.
`deno task test` — 165 passed, all six golden SVG hashes intact.
board-element — 189 passed, 4 skipped.
`deno task docs` — rebuilds every image byte-identically, tree clean.

`deno task verify` still exits 1 on `nx.json`'s missing trailing newline, which
predates this branch and is red on `main` too. Because `fmt` runs before `test`
in that `&&` chain, the task has not reached its tests since `905000c`. One byte,
and not this branch's to fix.

title: The board draws on the GPU
description:
The interactive board's SVG layer is replaced by a WebGL2 one. On the same
machine, the same board and the same movement, panning Insane 1000×1000
(85 809 pieces) goes from **1 050 ms a frame to 34 ms**, and building it from
2 761 ms to 338 ms.

Carries the design and the plan it was executed from:
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-10-webgl-board-layer-design.md` and
`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-10-webgl-board-layer.md`.

## Why not the cheaper options

A throwaway spike measured four renderers on one board before any of this was
written. Two of the three candidates the previous spec had named turned out to
be dead ends, and it took measuring to see it:

| renderer | preparation | pan mean |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SVG, as shipped | 2 761 ms, 429 055 nodes | 1 050.5 ms |
| Canvas 2D, culled to the view | 62 ms | 490.9 ms |
| Canvas 2D, one retained `Path2D` | 25 488 ms | 34.7 ms |
| **WebGL2, one static buffer** | **158 ms** | **16.5 ms** |

**Culling is not the lever; retention is.** The culled Canvas drew 15% of the
board and cost fourteen times more than the Canvas that drew all of it, because
it rebuilt its path every frame. **Removing the per-piece `<g>`** — the other
step the old spec named — would have taken 429 055 nodes to about 257 000, and
a renderer priced by the node count needed an order of magnitude, not 40%.

WebAssembly was considered and rejected on the same measurements: our own
JavaScript on the drawing path is 48 ms, once.

## What it looks like

`tesselate.ts` is pure and DOM-free, beside `viewport.ts` and `track.ts`: it
expands `pieceShape()` into triangles and hands back a map from piece id to its
slice of the buffer, so a removal or a ride touches one piece and never the
board. `gl-layer.ts` owns the canvas, two programs, the buffers and the
context-loss lifecycle. `view.ts` holds the types that used to live in the
renderer, so the public surface did not move when the renderer did.

One renderer for every board size, by decision — no hybrid, no SVG fallback for
small boards, because a threshold means two code paths and two visual results
for one product.

**The public API of `<arrowz-board>` is unchanged** apart from one addition,
`pieceCount`: with no DOM nodes there was no other way to ask a board how many
pieces it is drawing.

**The CLI's SVG export is untouched.** `geometry.ts`, `toSvg` and the golden
hashes stay exactly as they were; a file on disk and a canvas on screen have
different requirements, and only the second one had a problem.

## Numbers, and where they are honest

Measured in a foreground Chrome 152 on an M1 at devicePixelRatio 1, Insane
1000×1000 seed 7:

- build 338 ms, pan mean 34.0 ms (worst 73.5), zoom mean 33.3 ms (worst 34.9)
- GPU memory 79.2 MB monochrome, 118.7 MB once colours are switched on

**A runner without a GPU cannot measure this layer.** On the old headless shell
the same board panned at 789.6 ms, because two million triangles were rasterised
on the CPU. On the real Chrome engine this branch now runs against — the
environment #32 introduced — headless on an M1 reaches an actual GPU and the
gated Nightmare median is 16.7 ms. So the warning is about the absence of a GPU,
not about headless as such, and a Linux CI runner is the case it applies to.
Either way the perf test's frame times in a `verify` log are a relative
regression signal and nothing more, and the file says so.

For the same reason the Nightmare frame budget lives behind `ARROWZ_MEASURE=1`
rather than in `verify`. Asserting a wall-clock frame time inside a task runner
that saturates the machine measured the machine: five identical runs produced
medians from 77 to 337 ms while the build in those same runs stayed at 16-56 ms.
Behind the flag, on an idle machine, the median is 24.7 ms against a 50 ms
budget — the criterion the original spec chose.

**This has a consequence for #32**, which is open against `main` and adds
`expect(mean).toBeLessThan(50)` to this very test. That assertion has the same
defect and a mean is more contention-sensitive than the median that failed here
five times running; it should become the same deliberate-run assertion before
that PR merges.

## Known and deliberate

- **Tail roundings are about 40% of all geometry** at the ceiling — 1.37 M
  triangles of 3.46 M — and none of them are visible at the fitted zoom.
  `TAIL_SEGMENTS` is 16 because at devicePixelRatio 2 eight facets are plain to
  the eye. The way out is a signed-distance round cap in the fragment shader:
  six vertices instead of forty-eight, right at every zoom. It is named as the
  next step in §12 rather than done here, because reopening `tesselate.ts` would
  restart the review chain on the plan's most delicate file for a gain nobody has
  measured, and 34 ms already clears the criterion.
- **Accessibility is out of scope** by §2.6, and nothing regressed: the SVG
  carried no roles or labels either, and the chrome buttons are untouched DOM.
- `GlLayer` is 944 lines and grew by accretion over six tasks; the ride
  orchestrator is cleanly separable and should come out before the next feature.

## Verification

`pnpm nx run-many -t verify` green, eight consecutive uncached runs across two
machines' worth of load. 177 tests across the Node and browser projects.


---

## Merged `main` (2026-09-10)

#32 landed on `main` while this branch was in flight, and both edit
`perf.browser.test.ts`. The two additions do not overlap textually, so git
merged them into a file declaring `NIGHTMARE_PAN_MS` twice — green locally,
red on CI, which is the only place the merge was ever built.

Reconciled by hand: `main`'s environment change is kept whole (real Chrome
engine at `deviceScaleFactor: 2`, full Chromium in CI), this branch's assertion
placement is kept (one constant, on the median, behind `ARROWZ_MEASURE=1`).

That merge also flipped the browser tests from devicePixelRatio 1 to 2, which
they survived — they derive their sample coordinates from the drawing buffer
rather than assuming a ratio — and exposed one real dpr-dependent defect: at
dpr 2 the antialiased seam between the paper and the transparent canvas is a
low-alpha, premultiplied-dark pixel that the tests' ink helper counted as ink.
Fixed by raising the helper's alpha floor, not by touching the layer.

title: The perf test measures a browser that presents to a screen
description:
The browser test project measured on Playwright's headless shell — a stripped
binary that rasterises in software at one device pixel per CSS pixel. It now
runs on the real Chrome engine (`channel: 'chromium'`) at `deviceScaleFactor: 2`,
and Nightmare gains the pan assertion the file never had.

## Why

`perf.browser.test.ts` printed a frame time and asserted only the build. The
spec's 50 ms pan threshold was therefore a number someone read off a log, not a
gate: nothing in the suite would have gone red if panning had got ten times
slower.

Chasing that led to measuring the same board four ways. The result corrects an
assumption the file was built on.

## Measured

M1, host 800×800 at devicePixelRatio 2, Insane seed 7 (85 809 pieces, 429 055
nodes), the same scripted `zoomBy(3)` then `panBy(-3, -2)` per frame:

| environment | pan mean | build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| headless shell, dpr 1 (before) | 83 ms | 1 330 ms |
| real Chrome engine headless, dpr 2 (after) | 104 ms | 1 920 ms |
| Chrome 152 in the foreground, with a GPU | 1 050 ms | 2 761 ms |

The binary and the pixel density together account for 83 → 104 ms. The
remaining tenfold is raster and composite of 429 055 nodes onto a display,
which nothing headless pays for because it presents nothing. **No CI test can
gate the frame time a person sees.** The header now says so and carries all
three figures, so the next reader does not mistake a headless print for
reality.

Nightmare measures 16.6 ms in the new configuration — the rAF floor, so the
element may triple its per-frame work before the 50 ms budget bites. The
assertion was verified to fail: lowering the budget to 5 ms produces
`expected 16.58 to be less than 5`.

## CI

`playwright install` drops `--only-shell`, and the cache key names the browser
build. The lockfile does not change when that choice does, so without the
marker the shell-only cache would restore for ever and the full browser would
be downloaded on every run, never saved.

## Not in scope

The ceiling case is unusable in a real browser whatever this file prints, and
no budget fixes that — it needs a different drawing model. A throwaway spike
compared SVG against Canvas 2D and WebGL2 on this board; WebGL2 panned the
whole thing at 16.5 ms with no culling, against SVG's 1 050 ms. That is a
separate design round.

## Verification

`pnpm nx run-many -t verify` green across all three projects.

title: The demo grows an inspector, and the zoom stops moving the board under the cursor
description:
Three changes to `@arrowz/board-element`, from one session of driving the demo.

## The demo's inspector

The board sat beside a header of five checkboxes that reached four of the
element's nine inputs, and nothing said what the element was reporting back.
The header is gone; a panel beside the board lists every reflected attribute
and every field of `view`, drives the element directly with them, prints the
markup that would reproduce what is on screen, and logs the events as they
arrive.

- `demo/controls.ts` is one table of the element's inputs. The panel builds its
  controls from it and the snippet reads it to decide what to print, so a new
  property on `<arrowz-board>` is one row rather than three edits.
- The snippet prints only values that differ from the defaults — the shortest
  markup that reproduces the screen. Its tag line is read from
  `getAttributeNames()`, and a `MutationObserver` keeps both it and the controls
  honest when the demo changes an attribute behind the panel's back (losing the
  last life clears `play`, and the checkbox follows).
- The event console folds consecutive repeats into a count and drops muted types
  before the buffer. `viewport-change` starts muted: it fires once a frame while
  a drag is in flight and would otherwise flush the four game events out of the
  200-row log within a second of panning.

## The zoom holds the point under the cursor

`zoomAt` always computed the right origin and `clamp` threw it away — the centre
substituted on an axis with slack, and "the board must fill the view" near an
edge, which is the same as forbidding the anchor there. Measured on a 100x100
board, eight wheel steps into a corner walked the point **583 px** away from the
cursor it was supposed to be under.

The bound is now the middle of the view staying between the board's two margins.
Zooming towards a point pulls the view's centre towards it, so on the board the
bound never binds and the anchor is exact at every step; it still stops a pan
from leaving the board behind. `fit` names the centred origin itself.

Paid at the edges, with the trade-off taken deliberately: blank paper beside the
board when zooming into one, and a board smaller than the host no longer pinned
to the middle. `fit()`, `0`, the corner button and a double click restore it.

The old test asked whether the point stayed in the same *cell*, on a board whose
proportions left no slack on either axis, so neither half of the drift could
appear in it.

## The grab cursor answers the modifier

Holding ⌘ or Ctrl changed nothing until a button went down, so the cursor kept
promising a move while the next click would pan. The board now watches the
modifier from the moment the pointer arrives: keys off the window (a board is
rarely focused when a hand lands on ⌘), only while the pointer is over it, with
`blur` covering ⌘-Tab. The piece cursor is removed rather than outranked in the
cascade.

## Verification

`pnpm nx verify board-element`: 160 passed, 3 skipped; check, lint, fmt and
build clean. 23 of those tests are new for the demo's two pure modules (the node
project's include gained `demo/**/*.test.ts`), 3 are browser tests for the
cursor, and 3 pin the zoom anchor in full precision.

Checked by hand in Chrome as well: generation, a played piece, live snippet and
control edits, the event filters and folding, the cursor through a real ⌘ press,
and 0.0 px of drift on eight wheel steps.

title: Docs: the blocking arrow stands in a column, not on a grid line
description:
## What

In `docs/images/rule-blocked.svg` — the README picture for "something is standing in the lane" — the red arrow was drawn at `x=220`. The grid lines run at `20, 60, 100, …`, so cell centres are `40, 80, 120, …`: `220` is a line, not a centre. With `stroke-width="20"` the body covered `210–230`, spilling half a stroke into each neighbouring column, and the head (`208–232`) straddled the line and hid the tip of the grey arrow underneath it.

The arrow moves half a cell right, onto the centre at `x=240`. The neighbouring centre `x=200` was not free: the grey arrow's head already reaches `x=218` there. `240` is still inside the dashed lane (`x` 140–340), so the picture makes exactly the same point, and the head keeps the geometry the other two rule pictures use (24 px wide, 16 px long, tip stopping 2 px short of the next grid line, 2 px gap to the body).

## Rendering

`rule-blocked.png` is redrawn with `rsvg-convert -w 460 docs/images/rule-blocked.svg`. That is the command the rule pictures were made with: running it on the untouched `rule-free.svg` reproduces the committed `rule-free.png` byte for byte, so the new file matches the rest in scale (460x358) and renderer.

## Notes

Text is untouched; `README.md` and `README.pl.md` point at the same PNG.

title: Board element: <arrowz-board> on Lit, and the board plays the game
description:
Road map step 2: the `<arrowz-board>` web component.

## What is in the branch

- **`packages/board-element`** (`@arrowz/board-element`, Lit 3, no decorators): a thin Lit shell renders the chrome (zoom buttons, pan hint) around one `<svg>` owned by an imperative SVG layer. World units are cells; zoom and pan change only the root `viewBox`. Properties `board`, `view`, `interactive`, `lang`; methods `animateExit`, `shake`, `fit`, `zoomBy`; getter `viewport`; events `piece-click` and `viewport-change` (composed, coalesced per frame). Board updates diff by piece identity, so the game's next board costs one pass over ids. Pure modules `viewport.ts` and `gestures.ts` carry the §7/§8 rules of the game design and are tested in Node; the layer and the element are tested in Chromium (Vitest 5 browser mode, Playwright).
- **Engine**: `geometry.ts` (`DIRS`, `pieceShape`, `voidStrips`) extracted from `toSvg`; `toSvg` output is byte-identical, pinned by five SHA-256 golden hashes recorded before the extraction (`svg-golden.json`), the CLI byte-for-byte test and the fingerprints.
- **Tooling**: tsc emission to `dist/`, Nx targets (`check`, `lint`, `fmt`, `test`, `build`, `serve`, `verify`), the package as a package.json-only member of the Deno workspace so root `deno fmt`/`deno lint` govern it, CI installs the Chromium headless shell with a cached download.
- **Demo** (`pnpm nx serve board-element`): presets, generation in a worker, click = exit, ⇧ click = shake, scripted pan/zoom measurement, `lang=pl` switch.
- **Docs**: package README, spec §15 with the measured numbers, engine HISTORY entry.

## Measurements (headless Chromium 153, Apple M1)

| Board | Pieces | SVG nodes | Build | Pan mean / worst | Zoom mean / worst |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nightmare 100×100 | 915 | – | 15 ms | 16.6 / 17.8 ms (frame floor) | – |
| Insane 1000×1000 | 85 809 | 429 050 | 1 331 ms | 83.1 / 356.8 ms | 104.5 / 370.7 ms |

Acceptance of the spec (§11): Nightmare holds. Insane builds well under the 5 s budget but pans and zooms above the 50 ms frame threshold, so SVG stays for this step and the follow-up is a separate spec: drop the per-piece `<g>` (five nodes per piece today), re-measure, then decide between viewport virtualisation and Canvas. A manual run of the demo in a foreground window on the target machine should precede that decision.

## Verification

`pnpm nx run-many -t verify` green for engine, cli and board-element (19 tasks); `deno task verify` green (145 Deno tests); the package runs 60 Vitest tests (Node + Chromium) plus one env-gated Insane measurement.

## Rulings taken during execution

See the "Rulings I made" list in the session summary; the notable ones: the package is a Deno workspace member (fmt/lint discovery), CI installs Playwright through `pnpm --filter`, the Insane numbers come from headless Chromium through a test gated by `ARROWZ_MEASURE=1`, and the demo ships a `lang` switch instead of a hard-coded `lang="pl"`.


---

# The board plays the game (second body of work on this branch)

Spec `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-10-board-game-design.md`, plan `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-10-board-game.md`. Nineteen commits on top of the element above.

## What is in it

- **`packages/engine/game.ts`** — the reducer of game design §10, cut down to what a board can decide: move legality by a lazy ray scan (at most `max(W, H)` reads of an `Int32Array`), removal, the end of the board, and snapshots. Runtime-neutral, in the `NEUTRAL` list. `Board` is immutable for a session's lifetime; `Session.gone` is a `Uint8Array` copied per move, so §10's purity costs an 86 kB memcpy at the ceiling instead of a walk over a copied Set.
- **`packages/board-element/src/game-host.ts`** — a plain class owning one session and driving an injected target (`animateExit`, `shake`, `emit`), so the rules test in Node rather than through a browser. It clamps a zero-distance bounce to `MIN_SHAKE_CELLS`, because a blocker directly ahead would otherwise draw nothing and the bounce is what tells the player where the blocker is.
- **The element plays** — a `play` attribute (separate from `interactive`, so the lab keeps click-to-inspect), the events `piece-removed`, `life-lost` and `finished`, and `saveState()` / `loadState()` / `restart()`. Lives, the stopwatch and scoring stay with the host: the element counts nothing and `status` is only `'playing' | 'won'`.
- **A saved game** is `{ v, board: { W, H, pieces, fingerprint }, removed, colored }`. `fingerprint(board)` runs only on save and load, and `loadSession` gates on size and piece count before it — two million iterations at the ceiling.
- **Colours behind a permission** — `enable-colors` gates a fourth chrome button; without it the board is monochrome whatever `view.colored` says, because telling pieces apart without colour is the puzzle (§11). The per-piece hue now derives from `piece.id` rather than the array index, which also lets coloured boards use the identity diff.
- **A point grid** — `show-points`, `point-color`, `point-radius`. One `<pattern>` of one cell pitch plus one `<rect>`: two nodes whatever the board's size, where a `<circle>` per dot would be a million at the ceiling. The three inputs stay out of `BoardView` on purpose, because `sameView()` drives `canDiff` and a view field would rebuild 86 000 pieces per toggle. The grid hides itself below `MIN_POINT_CELL_PX` per cell.
- **Demo and docs** — the demo plays a game with lives, save, load and restart, and toggles the grid; the README covers every new input, method and event.

## Superseded within this branch

The paragraph above about the element diffing "the game's next board" no longer holds. The reducer does not produce boards: `Board` is immutable for a session, so assigning `board` starts a new game and redraws in full. Diffing by piece identity still governs everything else, and coloured boards joined that path. Recorded in the spec's §9 and noted in the step 2 design doc.

## Measurements (headless Chromium, Insane 1000×1000)

| What | Off | On |
|---|---|---|
| Verdict (`play()`, mean of 5 000 calls) | — | 0.0001 ms |
| Build with the point grid | 1 618.8 ms | 2 323.7 ms |
| Pan mean with the point grid | 80.2 ms | 77.2 ms |
| SVG nodes with the point grid | 429 055 | 429 056 |

The grid's +705 ms is a one-off first-paint cost for rasterising a pattern across a million cells; pan is unaffected and the node count confirms the design. It is accepted rather than optimised: the mode is opt-in and the visibility threshold already keeps the grid off the screen where the raster would be worthless.

## Verification

`pnpm nx run-many -t verify` green for engine, cli and board-element; 132 Vitest tests in board-element (Node + Chromium), 125 Deno tests in the engine, the golden SVG hashes and the fingerprints untouched.

## How it was built

Eight planned tasks, each executed by a fresh subagent and gated by its own review, then a whole-branch review and one fix wave. Five fix rounds, every one caused by a defect in the plan rather than the execution — four of them tests that passed while guarding nothing, including one that asserted the opposite of the risk it was written for. The whole-branch review caught the one that mattered most: the element's session lagged the `board` property by one Lit update, so `el.board = b; el.loadState(snap)` threw and `saveState()` could return a snapshot of the previous board. Fixed by reconciling the session at the entry points instead of on the framework's notification.

title: Build: monorepo with the engine and the CLI as workspace packages
description:
## Summary

- `prototype/` becomes two Deno workspace packages: `packages/engine` (`@arrowz/engine`, subpath exports `./command`, `./simple`, `./presets`, `./i18n`) and `packages/cli`; the CLI imports the engine by name. Every move is a `git mv`; `engine.ts`, `fingerprints.json` and `fingerprints.test.ts` are pure renames.
- pnpm workspace + Nx 23.2 at the root; the Deno packages are Nx projects through `run-commands`, with a local cache (`pnpm nx run-many -t verify` runs check, lint, fmt, test, the Node build and smoke of the engine and the lab bundle; a second run is served from the cache).
- The engine gets a Node build (`tsc` with `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, `nodenext`, declarations) and `scripts/node-smoke.mjs`, which reproduces the eight golden fingerprints (with piece counts and `maxLen`) from `dist/` under Node 24.
- Editor settings scope the Deno extension to the two packages; CI runs `pnpm nx affected -t check lint fmt test build smoke bundle` on pull requests and `main` (workflow and `pnpm-workspace.yaml` are Nx shared globals, so a CI-only change affects every project).
- Documentation follows: both READMEs, `CLAUDE.md`, an addendum in the 2026-09-07 design spec, a superseded banner on the old scaffold slice; `prototype/README.md` is now `packages/engine/HISTORY.md`.

Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-09-monorepo-design.md`. Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-09-monorepo.md`.

Branch was created from `main` with the still-open PR branches #25 (spec + plan) and #26 (agent skills) merged in; once those two are merged, this diff collapses to the monorepo commits.

## Verification

- Spikes (throwaway, `/tmp`): Deno runs silently next to a pnpm-owned `node_modules/` with `nodeModulesDir: "manual"`; `tsc` 5.9.3 emits the engine and Node reproduces the golden `voids` board.
- `deno task verify`: 134 tests, boards bit-identical (`fingerprints.test.ts`).
- `pnpm nx reset && pnpm nx run-many -t verify bundle`: green from a clean cache, second run from cache.
- `deno task carve --width=25 --height=50 --dry-run` from the root prints the golden `simple` fingerprint; `sh packages/cli/lab.sh` serves the lab and saves a board.
- `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` passes; a `tsc` consumer probe (`bundler`, `nodenext`, Angular-like settings, `skipLibCheck: false`) type-checks against `dist/` with no errors.
